sections.h2: Wisconsin tax on a home sale gain
sections.html:
Wisconsin has no separate capital gains tax. A gain on a house is taxed inside the regular individual income tax, and you may subtract 30 percent of a net long-term gain. The Department of Revenue's Publication 103 notes that the capital gain in Wisconsin income can differ from the federal figure, because Wisconsin allows a deduction for 30 percent of the net capital gain from assets held more than one year.

A seller therefore deals with two layers. The federal layer decides how much of the gain is taxable at all, home sale exclusion included. The Wisconsin layer begins with federal adjusted gross income and then applies its own adjustments, the 30 percent subtraction among them.

sections.h2: How much of the gain Wisconsin taxes
sections.html:
On a house held more than one year, Wisconsin taxes 70 percent of the net long-term gain left after the federal rules. The deduction is 30 percent of net capital gain from assets held more than a year, and 60 percent for farm assets held more than a year. Long-term means you owned the asset for more than one year; one year or less is short-term and gets no subtraction.

Whatever stays in Wisconsin taxable income is taxed at your marginal Wisconsin rate. A house owned for eleven months is short-term, so none of its gain gets the break.

The 60 percent rate is written for farm assets. A seller of an ordinary residence should plan on 30 percent. If you think the farm rate applies to you, read the Schedule WD instructions or ask the Department of Revenue.

The federal exclusion shields up to $250,000 of gain on a main home, or $500,000 on a joint return. Wisconsin income starts from federal adjusted gross income, so gain the exclusion removes never reaches the Wisconsin calculation. IRS Topic 701 gives the tests.

  • Ownership: you owned the home for at least 24 months out of the 5 years before the sale.
  • Use: you lived in it as your residence for at least 24 months of those 5 years. The two periods needn't be the same 24 months.
  • On a joint return, either spouse may meet the ownership test but both must meet the use test.
  • You generally can't use the exclusion if you excluded the gain on another home during the two years before this sale.

A Form 1099-S for the sale must be reported even if the whole gain is excludable, and you must report the sale if you can't exclude all of the gain. Remaining gain goes on federal Form 8949 and Schedule D. The exclusion covers a main home, so a rental or a house you never lived in has to be tested against the same two rules.

Wisconsin has four rates for 2025, from 3.5 percent to 7.65 percent, and a taxable gain is stacked on top of your other income. These brackets reflect 2025 Wisconsin Act 15.

RateSingle, head of householdMarried filing jointly
3.50%$0 to $14,679$0 to $19,579
4.40%$14,680 to $50,479$19,580 to $67,299
5.30%$50,480 to $323,289$67,300 to $431,059
7.65%$323,290 and up$431,060 and up

A large gain can push you into a higher bracket in the year of sale. The 70 percent left after the subtraction is the amount taxed at these rates. Brackets move with inflation and legislation, so use the table for the year you close.

sections.h2: Reporting the sale on a Wisconsin return
sections.html:
Individuals report the gain on Wisconsin Schedule WD, and the result flows to Schedule AD or Schedule SB of Form 1. An adjustment from Schedule WD goes on line 2 of Schedule AD, which is an addition, or line 5 of Schedule SB, which is a subtraction. The 30 percent deduction on a long-term gain lands on Schedule SB.

  • Residents file Form 1 with Schedule WD.
  • Nonresidents and part-year residents use Form 1NPR and follow its instructions.
  • A mutual fund or REIT capital gain distribution alone doesn't need Schedule WD on Form 1, though Form 1NPR filers still complete it.

A house that closes in 2026 belongs on the 2026 return, so use that year's forms.

sections.h2: If the house sells at a loss
sections.html:
A loss on a home you lived in isn't deductible, since losses on personal-use property such as a home or car aren't tax deductible. A loss on a rental house or other investment property can offset gains.

Wisconsin follows the same ceiling as federal law for capital losses. From tax year 2023, when losses exceed gains, up to $3,000 of the excess ($1,500 if married filing separately) may be deducted against other income, and the rest carries forward with no time limit. A Wisconsin carryover can differ from the federal one, so the Schedule WD figure may not match your federal return.

Gain on an inherited house is measured from the owner's basis, and IRS Publication 551 covers basis for inherited or gifted property. Property acquired from a decedent is also an exception to the usual test for deciding whether a gain is long-term, with details in Publication 544.

One Wisconsin difference exists. Land acquired by inheritance and valued differently for Wisconsin inheritance tax and federal estate tax purposes can carry a different basis, but that applies only to deaths before January 1, 1992. A recent inheritance doesn't raise the issue.

The federal bill is usually the larger one. For 2025 most net capital gain is taxed at no more than 15 percent, using these taxable income thresholds:

  • 0 percent rate: up to $48,350 for single filers and $96,700 for married filing jointly.
  • 15 percent rate: above those amounts up to $533,400 for single filers and $600,050 for married filing jointly.
  • 20 percent rate: above the 15 percent thresholds.

Short-term gain is taxed as ordinary income. Unrecaptured section 1250 gain on real property, which can arise on a rental after depreciation, is taxed at a maximum of 25 percent. High earners may also owe the net investment income tax described in IRS Topic 559, and a large gain can require estimated tax payments (Topic 409).

Wisconsin offers a deferral federal law lacks, but it is for investing in a qualified Wisconsin business, not for buying another house. A taxpayer may defer tax on a long-term gain invested in a qualified Wisconsin business within 180 days, using Schedule CG, and the basis in the new investment drops by the deferred gain. Long-term gain on such an investment held at least five uninterrupted years can qualify for exclusion from Wisconsin income.

An installment sale works differently. Federal default reports gain as payments arrive, and a Wisconsin election can differ from the federal one. If you will carry a note for the buyer, plan the reporting with a tax professional before signing the contract. A cash sale avoids the question, since you receive the full price at closing.

faqs.q: Does Wisconsin tax capital gains on a home sale?
faqs.a: Yes, as part of income. Wisconsin lets you subtract 30 percent of net long-term capital gain, and the federal home sale exclusion of up to $250,000 ($500,000 on a joint return) can remove the gain before Wisconsin sees it.

faqs.q: What is the Wisconsin capital gains deduction?
faqs.a: It is 30 percent of net capital gain from assets held more than one year, or 60 percent for farm assets held more than a year. Schedule WD computes it.

faqs.q: What are the Wisconsin income tax rates for 2025?
faqs.a: They are 3.5, 4.4, 5.3 and 7.65 percent. For a single filer the 5.3 percent bracket runs from $50,480 to $323,289, and 7.65 percent applies above $323,289.

faqs.q: Can I deduct a loss on a home I lived in?
faqs.a: No. Losses on personal-use property such as a home aren't deductible. A loss on a rental or investment house can offset capital gains, plus up to $3,000 of other income per year in Wisconsin.

faqs.q: Where do I report the sale on my Wisconsin return?
faqs.a: On Schedule WD, which feeds line 2 of Schedule AD or line 5 of Schedule SB of Form 1. Nonresidents and part-year residents use Form 1NPR.
